podcast.title: First Wave (1984-1994)
podcast.body: The first wave of emo spanned from approximately 1984 to 1994, a decade during which the genre was born and developed. Initially, emo was underground and not widely known. "That's the first wave of emo, a 10 year span during which emo was born and developed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Second Wave (1994 onwards)
podcast.body: The second wave of emo began in 1994, directly following the first wave. This period saw emo spread and evolve, incorporating more dynamics into songs with explosive screaming juxtaposed with quiet melodic sections. "The traditional hardcore community thought second wave emo groups and their fans were a bunch of whims. But at the same time, though, there were those who appreciated this raw, emotional honesty. Emo had not only spread, but it evolved."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Third Wave (2000-2010)
podcast.body: The third wave of emo, occurring in the early 2000s, represented "peak emo." It began around 2000, peaked around 2008, and started moving into the background by 2010. This period saw emo blow up into the mainstream and fragment into numerous variations, much to the annoyance of purists who often declared "that's not emo." "Third wave emo begins in 2000 and proceeds starting in about 2008 and moved into the background again as of around 2010. This is when things not only began to blow up in the mainstream but also splinter into a million different variations, something that really annoyed the purists. Forgive them if they screamed, that's not emo, about a bunch of acts that were being labeled emo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anti-Commercial Ethos in Second Wave
podcast.body: The second wave of emo largely maintained an underground and anti-commercial stance. It was considered "uncool" for bands to sell t-shirts at shows, cover charges for gigs were typically five dollars or less, and charging more than ten dollars for a CD was deemed "gouging." "And everything stayed underground and very anti-commercial. For example, if you were in an emo band, it was almost considered uncool to even sell t-shirts at your show. Covered charge for a gig had to be five bucks or less. And if you charge more than ten dollars for a CD, well, that was considered gouging."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakthrough and Pop-Punky Evolution (Late 1990s)
podcast.body: Emo experienced a significant breakthrough towards the end of the 1990s, evolving to become both poppier and punkier. This new iteration incorporated numerous hooks and melodies, making it more broadly appealing. "It was towards the end of the 90's when emo really began to break through. It became more poppy as well as punky. Lots of hooks and melodies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Catharsis of Emo Shows
podcast.body: Emo shows during the third wave provided a hugely cathartic experience for fans, allowing them to collectively express and scream out their pain and fear alongside hundreds or thousands of others. "Fans loved it. There was something hugely cathartic about being able to scream your pain and fear with hundreds or even thousands of people out of show."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Commercial Success and Major Label Interest (Third Wave)
podcast.body: Third wave emo bands operated in an era where commercial success was attainable. Major labels showed significant interest, hoping to position emo as "the next grunge," and radio stations actively played emo-ish music. Many emo records from bands like New Found Glory, Fall Out Boy, Panic! at the Disco, Taking Back Sunday, The All-American Rejects, Simple Plan, and Alexisonfire achieved top 10 album chart positions. "The one thing just about all these third wave emo bands had in common was that they lived in an era where commercial success wasn't impossible. Major labels were interested, very interested, in turning emo into the next grunge. Radio was interested and was playing a lot of emo-ish music. Emo records from bands like Newfound Glory, Fallout Boy, Patek at the Disco, Taking Back Sunday, All American Rejects, Simple Plan, and Alexis on Fire all rocketed into the top 10 on the album charts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comparison to Punk and Ska Revivals
podcast.body: Emo revivals are noted to differ from punk and ska revivals. Instead of undergoing a full period of hibernation before returning, emo has arrived in distinct, sometimes overlapping, waves. "emo is slightly different than the punk and sky revivals in that it has come at us in different waves instead of going into full-on hibernation for a while and then coming back."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dark Turn in Third Wave Lyrics
podcast.body: As third wave emo grew, some bands incorporated darker lyrical themes, including violent imagery, references to self-harm (like cutting), and hateful expressions directed at women. This content later became a source of concern and regret for fans and bands looking back. "Some bands dipped into writing lyrics that contained violent imagery, talk of self-harm, like cutting, and more than a few hateful stabs are doing harm to women. This became a real problem later when fans and bands look back at some of the music and said, what were we thinking?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline in Fashion (2010s)
podcast.body: Emo, which had been a driving force of punk pop a decade earlier, had largely gone out of fashion in the 2010s, contributing to pop punk's decline. "Third, emo, which had been a driving force of punk pop a decade earlier, had largely gone out of fashion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Decline of Third Wave Emo
podcast.body: Between 2000 and 2010, the emo market became saturated. The music began to feel stale, and as fans matured, their interest waned. Younger generations entering their coming-of-age years sought different sounds, gravitating towards pop, K-pop, and hip-hop, leading to a decline in emo's popularity. "There was a lot of emo for everyone between 2000 and 2010, but you know how music works, right? After a while it was just too much. Things to stale, the fans grew up and grew away. They weren't nearly as depressed. Younger fans now in their coming of age years wanted something different, and for them that was pop, K-pop specifically, and hip-hop, so interest-wained."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Definitional Debate
podcast.body: There is considerable debate regarding what constitutes emo and what does not, leading to divergent opinions on its boundaries and true origins. "And there's a lot of debate, and I mean a lot about what is and is not emo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early 2000s Peak, Early 2010s Decline, and Mid-2010s Revival
podcast.body: Emo experienced a peak in the early 2000s with bands like Dashboard Confessional, Saves the Day, Thursday, Story of the Year, Taking Back Sunday, and My Chemical Romance. By the early 2010s, it began to wane as fans matured and bands like Alexisonfire and My Chemical Romance disbanded, while others like Fall Out Boy, Paramore, and Panic! at the Disco moved away from their original emo sound. However, by the middle of the decade, a strong emo revival emerged, bringing back bands like Alexisonfire and My Chemical Romance, and introducing a new generation of groups, possibly with a 90s bent. "It had its moments early in the century with bands like Dashboard Conventional and saves the day, Thursday, store the year, taking back Sunday and my chemical romance." "But by the early 2010s, emo had begun to wane as fans grew up and moved on, and bands broke up." "By the middle of the 2010s, there were signs of a strong emo revival."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

podcast.title: Early 90s Mention
podcast.body: Early emo was mentioned as one of the many forms of Alt Rock that enjoyed moments in the sun during the 90s, indicating its presence and development within the diverse alternative scene of the decade. "We could have just as well mentioned, early emo, dream pop, math rock, post-hardcore, alt metal, alt country, Tweet Rock, contemporary Christian alternative music, and so many more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Characteristics and Hardcore Punk Roots
podcast.body: Emo, initially a subgenre of hardcore punk, was characterized as brooding, introspective, sensitive, troubled, empathetic, vulnerable, straight-edged, confessional, and emotional. It was a "shrinking violet" within Alt Rock, often hard to find and avoiding attention. "If Alt Rock had a shrinking violet, it was definitely emo, the brooding, introspective, sensitive, troubled, empathetic, vulnerable, straight edged, confessional, emotional, subgenre, and descended of, believe it or not, hardcore punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence of Emo Fashion
podcast.body: The second wave saw the emergence of a distinct emo fashion, characterized by horn-rimmed glasses, bead necklaces, sweater vests worn over dress shirts, dress pants, and white socks. All clothing items except the socks were typically in darker colors, contributing to a generally "nerdy" aesthetic. "Emo fashion began to emerge. Horn-rimmed glasses, bead necklaces, sweater vests over dress shirts with dress pants and white socks. Everything but the socks had to be in darker colors too. So in other words, pretty nerdy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fashion (Emo Kids)
podcast.body: The "emo kids" fashion is characterized by trademark swoopy hair, often styled with one long bang covering an eye. Clothing typically consists of black, dark, or mixed gray tones, frequently worn in layers, including T-shirts, plaids, and hoodies. Skinny jeans, sometimes ripped, are common, paired with popular shoe brands like Vans or Converse. Accessories such as glasses, pins, patches, necklaces, piercings, and tattoos are prevalent, and dark eyeliner is popular for all genders. "The look includes the trademark swoopy hair, sometimes with one long bang covering one eye, close or dark or a mix of gray, and put on lots of layers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Four Distinct Waves
podcast.body: Emo music has manifested in four distinct waves, which sometimes overlap. Each of these waves typically spans a period ranging from 8 to 12 years. "Emo has come through in four distinct waves that sometimes overlap, and each of these waves has periods that run anywhere from 8 to 12 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fourth Wave (2010s onwards)
podcast.body: The fourth wave of emo began as the third wave was declining, roughly between 2008 and 2010. For most of the 2010s, this wave largely remained underground and regional. It was sustained by bands like Modern Baseball, Basement, Touche Amore, Into It. Over It., The Hotelier, Pianos Become The Teeth, Just Friends, and The World Is A Beautiful Place & I Am No Longer Afraid To Die. "As third wave emo was falling apart between 2008 and 2010, the fourth wave was beginning. However, for most of the 2010s, this wave stayed mostly underground and regional, but it was kept alive by bands like Modern Baseball, Basement, Tuchet Amour, Intu Over It, the Hotelier, pianos become teeth, just friends."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Goth Leanings in Look
podcast.body: Some emo-ish bands emphasize Goth leanings, particularly through their visual style. "Some emo-ish bands emphasize their Goth leanings, especially with their look."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hardcore Influence
podcast.body: Emo is listed as one of the genres that has been significantly influenced by hardcore music since the 1980s. "we've seen the influence this music has had on metal and in creating post-hardcore music as well as skate punk and emo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hardcore Punk Roots with Emotional Focus
podcast.body: Emo originated from the hardcore punk scene in Washington, D.C., but its defining characteristic is its emphasis on emotional subject matter. Songs frequently explore themes of big breakups, feelings of not fitting in, and general adolescent angst, differentiating it from purely rebellious punk. "Its roots are in the hardcore punk scene of Washington, DC, but instead of rebelling against authority, emo is much more emotional."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of Third Wave Reunions on Fourth Wave
podcast.body: The reunion of commercially successful third wave emo bands, such as Alexisonfire and My Chemical Romance, who are releasing new music and performing for large crowds, may potentially provide a boost for fourth wave emo bands. "Meanwhile though, some of those third wave emo bands, the most commercially successful of all the waves, have reformed. They're putting out new music and they're touring before huge crowds. Will these third wave vets result in a leg up for fourth wave emo bands? Let's see."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence from Fugazi
podcast.body: The emo sound that emerged later took cues from bands like Fugazi, specifically their intense, DIY punk rock approach and Straight Edge philosophy. "This would later take cues from bands like Fugazi when the whole emo sound came around a little bit later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence from Joy Division
podcast.body: The sound and style of Joy Division are credited with contributing significantly to the development of Emo music. "Their sound and style contributed to everything from the development of Goth to industrial music to Emo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Influences and Evolution in Fourth Wave
podcast.body: Fourth wave emo bands draw inspiration from various sources, with some influenced by 90s emo, others developing their sounds independently, and still others incorporating emo elements with their unique twists. The potential for these bands to achieve mainstream consciousness in the 2020s remains uncertain. "Some of the bands are inspired by 90s emo. Others have come up with sounds independently of that. Still others have taken elements of emo and put their own twist on things. Will any of them explode into mainstream consciousness in the 2020s? Hard to say."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Late 90s Diversification and Accessibility
podcast.body: By the end of the 1990s, emo had diversified considerably in terms of sound and style. While traditional emo (maintained by bands like Fugazi) persisted, more bands incorporated catchy guitar hooks instead of droning strumming. Vocals became less screamy, and lyrics, though still emotional, were less dire, moving from depressed to melancholy, with some songs even sounding happy. This increased accessibility to a wider audience. "By the end of the 1990s, emo came in all sorts of different colors and shapes. Sure, there was traditional emo, Fugazi made sure they kept that alive. But more events were using catchy guitar hooks instead of the drony strumming. While a lot of arrangements still had that loud, soft, loud, soft dynamic, vocals started to become a little less screamy. Lyrix were still very emotional but not quite as dire. Some had moved up the scale from depressed to merely somewhat melancholy. And hey, some songs actually sounded downright happy. All this contributed to a situation where emo is more accessible, more palatable to more people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstream Breakthrough in the 2000s
podcast.body: Emo music achieved mainstream popularity during the first decade of the 21st century. This surge contributed to pop punk's continued momentum, with bands like My Chemical Romance introducing new twists to the genre. "Pop punk roared through the first five or seven years of the century, picking up steam when emo went mainstream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Success in the 2000s
podcast.body: Between the summer of 2002 and the end of the decade, numerous bands, including Dashboard Confessional, Jimmy Eat World, and My Chemical Romance, were grouped into the emo category and achieved major success, leading to a period where "it seriously seemed as if the whole world was going emo." "All of them, for better or for worse, were clumped into the emo category, and they all had major success between the summer of 2002 and the rest of the decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Evolution in Second Wave
podcast.body: During the second wave, emo bands introduced greater dynamics into their songs, featuring loud, explosive screaming segments interspersed with quiet, melodic passages. "Bands began to put more dynamics into their songs, large, how'd explosive screaming bits, interspersed with quiet melodic parts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Variations
podcast.body: Emo exhibits a range of musical styles, from simple and straightforward compositions to more complex forms featuring unusual song structures and intricate guitar work. "Some emo is pretty simple and straightforward. Other flavors are more complex with unusual song structures and intricate guitar work."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: MySpace Artist Style
podcast.body: Emo was identified as one of the distinctive styles associated with "MySpace Artists." The platform's direct artist-to-fan interaction fostered communities around genres like emo, contributing to their popularization and the launch of new acts. "Before long, we had something called MySpace Artists, a distinctive set of styles that involved pop punk, emo, and indie acts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: Naming Controversy ("Emo Core")
podcast.body: The term "emo core" began circulating in the mid-1980s but was almost universally despised by the musicians who practiced the genre, with no one wanting to take credit for it. The shortened term "emo" eventually stuck as a way to classify the music. "The term started to be bandied about in the mid 1980s, but no one has really taken credit for it because no one liked it. The original term was emo core, which was almost universally despised by all practitioners of this music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Niche Genre Status
podcast.body: When Alexis on Fire was forming (around 2000-2001), Emo was not a mainstream genre but existed in "little pockets." Fans had to actively seek it out and connect with others who shared the same musical interests, often through underground shows and independent record stores. "Well, because Emo was not a thing. What? Emo was not a thing. Well, it was just, it was all in these little pockets and if you could find it, that was the thing too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Original D.C. Scene Dissolution
podcast.body: The original D.C. emo scene, prominent around 1988 and largely confined to the Washington D.C. area and bands on the Discord label, had completely dissolved by that year, with all involved bands breaking up and moving on. "However, this original DC emo scene was completely over by about 1988. All the bands involved had broken up and moved on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins Debate
podcast.body: The origin of emo is a tricky subject with very divergent opinions, with some researchers even tracing its roots back to The Beach Boys' "Pet Sounds" album in 1966. "And even this is a tricky subject because there are some very divergent opinions on who was responsible for this whole thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins and Mainstream Rise
podcast.body: Emo had its roots in the American Underground Hardcore punk scene of the 1980s but began to bubble up into the mainstream by the late 1990s. Its breakthrough was characterized by bands applying pop sensibilities to emotional themes of heartbreak and loss, making it more marketable and appealing. "Now Emo had its roots in the American Underground Hardcore punk scene of the 1980s. But by the late 1990s, it had begun to bubble up towards the mainstream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Origins as Emotional Hardcore
podcast.body: Emo is an offshoot of a particular type of hardcore punk that originated in the Washington D.C. area in the mid-1980s. It was originally known as Emotional Hardcore, or Emocore, characterized by loud, often screaming music grounded in sensitivity, anxiety, shyness, and heavy emotion. "Emo is an offshoot of a particular type of hardcore punk that originated in the Washington DC area in the middle 80s. Its original name was Emotional Hardcore, or Emocore for short, or just plain emo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins in Hardcore
podcast.body: Hardcore music is noted for pointing in the direction of what would become emo as early as the mid-1980s, with Minor Threat being a specific example. "Minor Threat pointed in the direction of what would become emo as early as the mid-1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pinkerton's Influence
podcast.body: The album "Pinkerton," initially misunderstood, is now "very well regarded and considered very influential, especially with the emo scene." "Now though, it's very well regarded and considered very influential, especially with the emo scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rivers Cuomo and Weezer - Alt-Rock's Nerd Heroes Part 1

podcast.title: Post-9/11 Explosion in Popularity
podcast.body: Emo remained a niche genre until after the traumatic events of September 11th, after which emo bands experienced an explosion in popularity for several years. Despite some bands not embracing the label, emo was pervasive in the early 2000s. "Emo stayed in its own corner of the alternative universe until after the traumatic events of 9-11. For the following several years, emo bands exploded in popularity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-9/11 Resonance
podcast.body: After the events of September 11, 2001, music infused with anguish, such as Emo, seemed particularly relevant and necessary. This context likely amplified the genre's appeal and contributed to its subsequent surge in popularity. "And after the events of 9-11, music with anguish seemed to be necessary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Revival in the Mid-2010s
podcast.body: Emo music came back into fashion around the mid-2010s, experiencing a revival alongside punk, shoegaze, and psychedelic music. "About a decade later, there was another revival. Straight ahead, punk came back into fashion as did emo, shoegays, and various flavors of psychedelic music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rock Subtype
podcast.body: Emo is listed as one of the many subtypes that rock music diversified into over the decades. "punk, metal, Prague, country rock, industrial, grunge, crock, rock, emo"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shift Towards Melodicism
podcast.body: Blink 182's "Enema of the State" had a significant effect on Emo, causing Emo bands to move away from super intense, hardcore-influenced punk towards more melodic and poppy styles. "Emo bands moved away from being super intense hardcore influence punk bands to being more melodic and poppy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 2

podcast.title: Short-Lived Trend (2000s)
podcast.body: Emo was an alt-rock trend that burned intensely but had a relatively short lifespan. By 2009, most rock fans had grown tired of it and moved on, indicating its rapid peak and subsequent decline within the music landscape. "Emo was one of those alt rock trends that burned very hot and very bright. And it didn't last very long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Subculture and Fashion
podcast.body: The rise of Emo music led to the creation of a distinct Emo subculture, complete with its own fashion, hairstyles, and language. For a period, it seemed that nearly every new band was labeled Emo, highlighting its widespread cultural impact. "The Emo subculture was created to service all this with its own fashion and hairstyles and language."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Subgenre Fragmentation
podcast.body: Emo became so popular that it began to cleave off and form new subgenres, including Emo Pop and Emo Rap, as well as regional variations like North Carolina emo, Midwest emo, and Aussie emo. "The emo thing got so big that bits of it cleaved off to form new subgenres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Emo Tremble and Tap
podcast.body: In contrast to slam dancing or mashing, emo developed its own unique dance styles. The "emo tremble" involved ringing one's hands while bouncing on the balls of the feet in time with the music, with a variation called the "emo tap" where one taps their chest to the rhythm. "Because emo wasn't about slam dancing or mashing, a new thing developed. The emo tremble. Basically, you ring your hands while bouncing off the balls of your feet in time with the music. A variation of that is sometimes called the emo tap, where you tap your chest along with the music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Thematic Influence on Emo Rap
podcast.body: Emo's characteristic themes and emotional feel are a direct influence on Emo Rap, contributing to its personal and vulnerable lyrical content. "Basically, we get all of Emo's hits when it comes to themes and feels, made it with hip hop, very personal, very vulnerable stuff, heartbreak, fear, anxiety, depression, loneliness."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 3: The New Genres

podcast.title: Third Wave Crossover and Fragmentation
podcast.body: The third wave was characterized by a crossover between "proper emo" and emo-like bands that were also classified as punk, pop punk, post-hardcore, and metalcore. This resulted in significant fragmentation, producing subgenres like emo-pop and screamo. Many third wave bands, some of whom had existed for years, achieved mainstream impact only in the early 2000s. "There was, in short, a crossover between proper emo, if you'll allow me to use that term, an emo-like bands, who were probably best classified as punk, pop punk, post-hardcore, and metalcore. There's a lot of fragmentation. Emo-pop, screamo bands, just a couple of examples. And not all third wave emo bands were brand new, some had been around for years. It was only in the early 2000s that they came of age and started making an impact beyond a small scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Underground Gestation and Stereotypes
podcast.body: Emo culture developed underground throughout the 1980s and 1990s, leading to the creation of the stereotypical "emo kid" image, complete with black hair, long bangs, black clothes, and thick-rimmed glasses. The genre also became associated with stigmas like depression and self-harm. "Emotional culture gestated underground through the 80s and 90s, resulting in the creation of the stereotypical emo kid with his or her black hair, the long bangs, the black clothes, the glasses with the thick rims."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
